  geom_point(<YOUR CODE PLOTTING RELATED IBD PAIRS>) +
  labs(<x, y, title, and subtitle text>) +
  guides(color = guide_legend("relatedness"))






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the complete solution to this exercise:

ibd_unrel <- filter(ibd_sum, rel == "none")
ibd_rel <- filter(ibd_sum, rel != "none")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = ibd_unrel, aes(x = total_ibd, y = n_ibd), color = "lightgray", size = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = ibd_rel, aes(x = total_ibd, y = n_ibd, color = rel)) +
  labs(
    x = "total IBD sequence",
    y = "number of IBD segments",
    title = "Total IBD sequence vs number of IBD segments",
    subtitle = "Both quantities computed only on IBD segments 10 cM or longer"
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(title = "relatedness"))












As a bonus, and to learn another parameter of aes() useful for scatter plots, in addition to setting color = rel (which sets a color of each point based on the relatedness value), add also shape = rel. Observe what happens when you do this!
Finally, I’m not personally fan of the default grey-filled background of ggplots. I like to add + theme_minimal() at the end of my plotting code of many of my figures, particularly when I’m creating visualizations for my papers. Try it too!






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the complete solution to this exercise:

ibd_unrel <- filter(ibd_sum, rel == "none")
ibd_rel <- filter(ibd_sum, rel != "none")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = ibd_unrel, aes(x = total_ibd, y = n_ibd), color = "lightgray", size = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = ibd_rel, aes(x = total_ibd, y = n_ibd, color = rel, shape = rel)) +
  labs(
    x = "total IBD sequence",
    y = "number of IBD segments",
    title = "Total IBD sequence vs number of IBD segments",
    subtitle = "Both quantities computed only on IBD segments 10 cM or longer"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(title = "relatedness"),
    shape = guide_legend(title = "relatedness")
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Visualization with ggplot2
section: Bonus Part 2: Practicing visualization on time-series data
text:
Bonus Part 2: Practicing visualization on time-series data

Exercise 8: Getting fresh new new data
We’ve spent a lot of time looking at metadata and IBD data, demonstrating various useful bits of techniques from across tidyverse and ggplot2. There are many more useful things to learn, but let’s switch gears a little bit and look at a slightly different kind of data set, just to keep things interesting.
First, create a new script and save it as f4ratio.R.
Then add the following couple of lines of setup code, which again loads the necessary libraries and also reads a new example data set:

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

f4ratio <- read_tsv("https://tinyurl.com/simgen-f4ratio", show_col_types = FALSE)

This data set contains results from a huge population genetics simulation study I recently did, and contains estimates of the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry in a set of European individuals spanning the past 50 thousand years.
Here’s a brief description of the contents of the columns:

individual, time – name and time (in years before present) of an individual
statistic – a variant of an estimator of Neanderthal ancestry
proportion – the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry estimated by statistic
rate_eur2afr – the amount of ancient migration (gene flow) from Europe to Africa in a given scenario
replicate – the replicate number of a simulation run (each scenario was run multiple times to capture the effect of stochasticity)


head(f4ratio)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  individual  time statistic       proportion rate_eur2afr replicate
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>                <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 eur_1      40000 direct f4-ratio   0.00687             0         1
2 eur_2      38000 direct f4-ratio   0.00807             0         1
3 eur_3      36000 direct f4-ratio   0.00192             0         1
4 eur_4      34000 direct f4-ratio   0.0245              0         1
5 eur_5      32000 direct f4-ratio   0.000390            0         1
6 eur_6      30000 direct f4-ratio  -0.00267             0         1


In other words, each row of this table contains the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry estimated for a given individual at a given time in some scenario specified by a given set of other parameters (rate_eur2afr, replicate).
In this exercise, I will be asking you some questions, the answers to which you should be able to arrive to by the set of techniques from tidyverse you’ve already learned, and visualize them using the ggplot2 functions you already know. When a new function will be needed, I will be dropping hints for you along the way!
This exercise is primarily intended for you to practice more ggplot2 visualization, because I think this is the most crucial skill in doing any kind of data analysis. Why? The faster you can get from an idea to a visualization of that idea, the faster you’ll be able to do research.
Let’s go!

Use geom_point() to plot the relationship between time (x axis) and proportion of Neanderthal ancestry (y axis). Don’t worry about any other variables just yet (colors, facet, etc.).
Note: The f4ratio table is too huge to plot every single point. Before you %>% pipe it into ggplot(), subsample the rows to just 10% of it subset using this trick:
f4ratio %>%
  sample_frac(0.1) %>% # subsample 10% fraction of the data
  ggplot(aes(...)) +
    geom_point()
Hint: Look at ?sample_frac but also ?sample_n and check out their parameters. They are incredible useful for any kind of data exploration!






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
sample_frac(0.1) %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion)) +
  geom_point()












Your plot now mashes together proportion values from two different statistic estimators. Fix this by facetting the plot, which will visualize both statistics in two separate panels. For the time being, keep doing the 10% subsampling step.
Hint: You can do this by adding + facet_wrap(~ statistic) to your previous code.






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
sample_frac(0.1) %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic)












Take a look at the values on the x-axis of your figure. Purely for aesthetics, it is customary to visualize time going from oldest (left) to present-day (right). But, currently, the time direction is reversed. Fix this by adding a new layer with + scale_x_reverse()!






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
sample_frac(0.1) %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse()












Whenever we visualize some biological statistics, we often want to compare their values to some kind of baseline (or a null hypothesis) value. In our case we have two:

The baseline of “no Neanderthal ancestry” at y-axis value 0,
The baseline of “known proportion of Neanderthal ancestry” today, which is about 3% (so y-axis value of 0.03).

Add those two baselines to your figure using a new function geom_hline() (standing for “horizontal line”). Like this:
<YOUR TIDYVERSE AND GGPLOT2 CODE ABOVE> +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", linetype = "dotted")
Note: You can immediately see the possibilities for adjusting the visuals like colors or linetype. Feel free to experiment with this!






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
sample_frac(0.1) %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = "dotted")












There’s clearly a huge amount of statistical noise, represented particularly in the “indirect f4-ratio” figure. And we’re not even plotting all points because there’s just too many of them!
Additionally, what I cared about in this particular case (during my PhD) were not values for each individual person (each represented by a single dot in the figure), but about the statistical trend in my data. An extremely important function for this is geom_smooth(), which fits a line through the data, capturing this trend.
In this next part, remove the subsampling done by sample_frac(), and also replace your geom_point() call in your figure code with this: + geom_smooth(se = FALSE). What happens when you run this modified version of your code? Read ?geom_smooth to figure out what se = FALSE means.






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = "dotted")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'













Well, we removed a lot of noise but we also removed most of the interesting signal! This is because we are now basically “smoothing” (averaging) over a very important variable: the amount of migration from Europe to Africa (which was the primary research interest for me at the time). Let’s take a look at our table again:

head(f4ratio)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  individual  time statistic       proportion rate_eur2afr replicate
  <chr>      <dbl> <chr>                <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 eur_1      40000 direct f4-ratio   0.00687             0         1
2 eur_2      38000 direct f4-ratio   0.00807             0         1
3 eur_3      36000 direct f4-ratio   0.00192             0         1
4 eur_4      34000 direct f4-ratio   0.0245              0         1
5 eur_5      32000 direct f4-ratio   0.000390            0         1
6 eur_6      30000 direct f4-ratio  -0.00267             0         1


What we want is to plot not just a single line across every single scenario, but we want to plot one line for each value of our variable of interest, rate_eur2afr.
Let’s add the variable into play by adding color = rate_eur2afr into your aes() call in the ggplot() function so that it looks like this: ggplot(aes(time, proportion, color = rate_eur2afr))
Note: You’ll get a warning which we will fix in the next step, don’t worry!






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion, color = rate_eur2afr)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = "dotted")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'


Warning: The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation:
colour.
ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
  the data.
ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
  variable into a factor?
The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation:
colour.
ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
  the data.
ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
  variable into a factor?









Don’t worry about the warning, we’ll fix this soon!




The reason we got a warning here is a slightly confusing behavior of the smoothing function geom_smooth(). Because rate_eur2afr is a numerical variable, the smoothing function cannot plot a single smoothed line for each of its values, because there could be (theoreticaly) an infinite number of them.
Fix the problem by adding group = rate_eur2afr right after the color = rate_eur2afr aesthetic mapping which you added in the previous exercise. This explicitly instructs geom_smooth() to treat individual values of rate_eur2afr as discrete categories.






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion, color = rate_eur2afr, group = rate_eur2afr)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = "dotted")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'













Let’s finalize our figure for publication! Use labs() to add proper x, y, and title descriptions (something like “Neanderthal ancestry proportion”, “years before present”, and “Expected Neanderthal ancestry trajectories”).
Don’t forget about the title of the legend too, which you can adjust by + guides(color = guide_legend("EUR -> AFR\nmigration")).
Finally, add my favourite + theme_minimal() at the end.






NoteClick to see the solution






f4ratio %>%
ggplot(aes(time, proportion, color = rate_eur2afr, group = rate_eur2afr)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.03, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Neanderthal ancestry proportion",
       y = "years before present",
       title = "Expected Neanderthal ancestry trajectories",
       subtitle = "Results from a set of population genetic simulations") +
  guides(color = guide_legend("EUR -> AFR\nmigration")) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'












And that concludes the recreation of one of my “famous” PhD-era figures. It demonstrated that various statistics estimating the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry in Europe across tens of thousands of years can reveal false (nonexistent) decline over time due to various (unaccounted for) demographic factors. It also showed that one particular statistic, since then named “direct \(f_4\)-ratio statistic” is robust to these problems, and that statistic remains in use to this day. We now know that Neanderthal ancestry levels in Europe remained stable for tens of thousands of years.

I hope that you now appreciate how adding little bits and pieces, one step at a time, makes it possible to create beautiful informative visualizations of any kind of tabular data!

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Advanced exercises
If you’ve already been introduced to ggplot2 before and the exercises above were too easy for you, here are a couple of additional challenges:

Take a look at how the ggridges package can potentially improve the readability of many density distributions when plotted for several factors ordered along the y-axis. For instance, how could you use this package to visualize the (admittedly practically useless, but still) distributions of longitudes (on the x-axis) for all samples in our metadata, ordered along the y-axis by the country? Note that you might also need to learn about ordering factors using the R package forcats.

As an extra challenge, try to make this figure as beautiful, colorful, and magazine publication-ready using ggplot2 theming

Study how you could turn our visualization of total IBD vs number of IBD segments as a function of the degree of relatedness into a proper interactive figure using ggplotly. For instance, make an interactive figure which will show the exact count and total IBD, as well as the names of individuals upon hovering over each data point with a mouse cursor.

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
“Take home exercise”
Take your own data and play around with it using the concepts you learned above. If the data isn’t in a form that’s readily readable as a table with something like read_tsv(), please talk to me! tidyverse is huge and there are packages for munging all kinds of data. I’m happy to help you out.
Don’t worry about “getting somewhere”. Playing and experimenting (and doing silly things) is the best way to learn.
For more inspiration on other things you could do with your data, take a look at the dplyr cheatsheet and the ggplot2 cheatsheet. You can also get an inspiration in the huge gallery of ggplot2 figures online!

title: Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Additional resources
As with our introduction to tidyverse, there’s so much more to ggplot2 than we had a chance to go through. I hope we’ll get through some spatial visualization features of R (which are tightly linked with tidyverse and ggplot2 in the modern R data science landscape), but there’s much more I wish we had time to go through.
Here are a couple of resources for you to study after the conclusion of the workshop, or even during the workshop itself if you find yourself with more time and more energy to study.

Factors are both a curse and blessing. When dealing with visualization, often a curse, because our factors are rarely ordered in the way we want. If our factors are numerical but not straightforward numbers (like our age_bin column above), their order in ggplot2 figures is often wrong. forcats is an incredible package which helps with this. Read about it in this vignette and then experiment with using it for figures in this session which featured factors.
cowplot is another R package that’s very useful for complex composite figures. We touched upon it in this session, but only extremely vaguely. Study this introduction to learn much more about its features! You will never need Inkscape again.
ggridges is a very cool package to visualize densities across multiple categories. It can often lead to much more informative figures compared to overlapping geom_density() plots we did in our session. Here’s a great official introduction to the package.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Preparation
A couple of points before we start this chapter.
library(slendr)
init_env()

title: Building slendr models
text:
Every one of your solutions for each exercise should contain these two lines of code. If you get errors about missing functions, simulation failures, etc., make sure your script starts with these lines.



Always write your solution in a dedicated script as instructed by each exercise. Don’t write everything into a single long file. Don’t run your code solution only in your R console without having them recorded in a script.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Forward direction of time
Create a new R script and saved it as slendr_models_forward.R. Write your solutions to this exercise into that script.

Encode the demographic model sketched in the following diagram using a series of population() calls, then compile it with compile_model(), storing it in the model variable. Finally, verify the correctness of the model visually using using the function plot_model().
Hint: Try to get into the habit of executing each command you add to your script (a line of code, a couple of lines, etc.) in your R console by pressing Ctrl (or Cmd)+Enter as you’re writing your solutions.


Note: At this moment, the time value has a completely arbitrary unit to be determined later. Additionally, unless otherwise specified, the size N will always indicate the “effective population size” \(N_e\).






NoteClick to see the solution





As always, we start our new script by loading slendr itself and activating its environment:

library(slendr)
init_env()

Adding to the script, we begin by creating the first population, called p1, storing it in a variable with the same name. When we execute this line and type p1 in the R console, we get an informative summary. Especially when building very complex models with slendr, it pays off to develop the habit to program models like this, one command at a time, always making sure that what we are programming matches what we want to program!

p1 <- population("p1", time = 1, N = 1000)

p1

slendr 'population' object 
-------------------------- 
name: p1 
non-spatial population
stays until the end of the simulation

population history overview:
  - time 1: created as an ancestral population (N = 1000)


Here is, then, the complete solution:

library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 1, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 100, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 200, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 300, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 401)

plot_model(model)












What happens when you don’t specify the simulation_length argument of the compile_model() function? Do you get an error if you leave out this argument? Why?






NoteClick to see the solution






model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

Error:
! The specified model implies a forward direction of time. However,
forward models require that the 'simulation_length' parameter is explicitly
specified in order to know when to terminate the simulation. If you
intended to run a backward time model instead, you can state this by
setting `direction = 'backward'.`


Notice that we did not yet run any (potentially computationally costly) simulation and slendr gave us an informative error message as soon as it encountered a potential error in our code. Again, this is a very strong argument for developing slendr models step by step, executing individual commands one after another, “conversing” with the R console in a way which lets slendr catch our mistakes as early as possible.
This is opposed to the other way of working, in which we would first write an entire (potentially very long) script and then potentially have trouble identifying where and how we made a mistake.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Backward direction of time
Unlike most other simulation frameworks, slendr gives us a lot of flexibility in how to encode the time units of our models, or even the direction of time used by our models.

Create a new R script and saved it as slendr_models_backward.R. Write your solutions to this exercise into that script.

Convert your forward model into using a backward direction of time (i.e., the model will implicitly end at time 0—“the present day”—and start at the appropriate “time ago”). You can start by copying the contents of slendr_models_forward.R into your new script, and modify its features accordingly. Again, visualize the final model using the plot_model() function, which should get you (visually) exactly the same figure.






NoteClick to see the solution





To solve this exercise, we simply have to take the total length of our original forward simulation and reverse the times of schedules event accordingly.
Note that this is very annoying to do—and it is what’s necessary to do with many frameworks other than slendr. This convenient flexibility of slendr becomes even more apparent once we start dealing with more realistic time units.

library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 400, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 300, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 200, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 100, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

plot_model(model)








Indeed, when we compare both figures side by side, we see that the forward and backward versions of the two model give the same figure (except for the “direction” of time units along the y-axis):













In the previous exercise, leaving out the simulation_length argument resulted in an error. Do you get an error when you leave it out this time? Why? Or why not?






NoteClick to see the solution





As we can see in our solution, leaving out simulation_length = 400 did not give an error this time because models encoded in “backward time units” naturally end at time 0 (i.e., “the present day”). This means that setting this argument works (we can still do it), but it’s redundant:

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 400)





What happens when you set this argument to a number that is shorter than the intended duration of the model in the schematic at the beginning, like setting simulation_length = 120? What would this imply about our programmed model?






NoteClick to see the solution





On the other hand, if we do set it to a smaller number, we effectively “truncate” the duration of the model. This is arelatively rare thing to do, but it could be useful in some circumstances, so it’s worth mentioning here:

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 120)

plot_model(model)








We can again compare the two models side by side to see the truncation more clearly:









Note: As I’m writing this solution, I just noticed that the colorscheme is wrong between the two visualization. That’s a huge benefit of teaching—it puts me into situations and applications I wouldn’t normally encounter! In fact, many improvements and new slendr features I introduced over the years have come up during teaching. Fixing this is already on my list of improvements.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Custom time units
For more theoretical or general models, specifying time in generations going forward (or backward) is generally enough. However, in more empirical settings, encoding times in other units can be quite handy. For instance, imagine you work with ancient DNA samples assigned with radiocarbon dates which use units of “years before the present”. Having to manually convert such times into generations gets cumbersome quickly, both when programming models and when analyzing simulated sequence data.
This is where the generation_time argument of compile_model() comes into the picture—with this argument, we instruct slendr on how should the various “genetic time numbers” in our model code interpreted as “real-world numbers”. Additionally, there’s another optional argument called time_units which we can use to give the numbers an explicit description.

In a new script slendr_models_human.qmd add a copy of your “backwards time” model code from above, then change it so that the time units can be interpreted as “years before present (BP)”, using the approximate human generation time of 30 years. Then visualize the model again to make sure you’ve programmed everything correctly.
Hint: You will want to modify the times of all demographic events in your model—originally in units of generations—so that they are effectively 30-times larger (so that the times represent human generation times), and make them run from larger values to smaller values (so that they represent units “years before present (BP)”). Finally, for clarity, you might want to use the time_units argument of compile_model() to give the units this description.






NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  generation_time = 30,
  time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model)








Again, when we compare this model to the very first model (which used time units of generations running forward in time), we see that they are completely identical—only the presentation changes (giving us much more convenience), but the population genetics theory underlying this model remains the same!

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Programming gene flow
Of course, real-world populations don’t just split from one another or change their size. Another common demographic process is gene flow (also called admixture or introgression in various context and in different species).
Modify your slendr_models_human.qmd script by using the function gene_flow() to program admixture from population “p2” into population “p3” starting at time 3000 “years B.P.”, with an end at time 2200 “years B.P.”. Set the total proportion of the “p2” ancestry in “p3” at 0.1 (i.e., 10% of the final “p3” population will be derived from “p2”).






NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)












When you look at ?gene_flow help page, you can see that the function has a migration_rate argument. What does it do? Is there any way to get the same result (i.e., to encode the same gene-flow event) as you did just above, but using rate instead of proportion? When would you expect to use one or the other?






NoteClick to see the solution





A 10% proportion of p2 ancestry derived from p3 over the time window of 3000 to 2100 years B.P. is mathematically equivalent to a per-year rate of 0.1 / (3000 - 2100), i.e. 1.1111111^{-4}. To express this in a slendr model, take a look at the modified call to gene_flow() below:

library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

year_rate <- 0.1 / (3000 - 2100)
gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, migration_rate = year_rate)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Common slendr errors
As noted above, slendr is designed around interactive use, executing little bits of code at a time, making sure that potential errors are caught as soon as we make them, rather than after spending lots of time programming long simulation scripts.
However, software errors often confuse new programmers, especially because most errors represent completely trivial typos and unintended mistakes rather than conceptual issues with our model’s logic. This is why it’s a good idea to spend a few moments to study the most common errors recognize why they occur in isolated, controlled settings.

First, let’s do a bit of a setup using things you already know. Create a new script called slendr_models_errors.R, just to have a “throwaway script” to experiment in without breaking your other working code.

Create an R variable pop containing a slendr population (using the population() function) with the name “pA”, at time 1 and with the \(N_e\) of 5000. Then, create a population “pB” of the same size, which splits from “pA” at time 100..






NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

pA <- population("pA", time = 1, N = 5000)
pB <- population("pB", time = 100, N = 5000, parent = pA)




When you do this, slendr automatically infers that you intend to specify time in your model flowing in the forward direction (i.e., times of events move from smaller numbers to larger numbers). Not only that, from this point on, slendr also enforces all following demographic events to follow this time direction!
To see how this works, create a third population named “pC”, which splits from “pB” at time 80. What does slendr do when you do this? What’s the closest appropriate value of pC’s split time which would be consistent with slendr’s assumptions for the direction of time for this model?






NoteClick to see the solution





We get an error because in the context of the model so far (pA starting at time 1 and pB splitting from it at time 100), pC would effectively split at an earlier time than it’s parent!

pC <- population("pC", time = 80, N = 5000, parent = pB)

Error:
! The model implies forward time direction but the specified split
time (80) is lower or equal to the parent's (100)


We can see that even setting the split time of pC to time 100 doesn’t work, because slendr enforces that a population can only split from its parent population at the time the latter already exists in the model:

pC <- population("pC", time = 100, N = 5000, parent = pB)

Error:
! The model implies forward time direction but the specified split
time (100) is lower or equal to the parent's (100)


In other words, the earliest that pC can split is time 101:

pC <- population("pC", time = 101, N = 5000, parent = pB)





As another example, let’s look at gene_flow(), which programs gene flow between two populations represented by two R variables. Let’s say that you try to program:

42% gene flow from pA to pC starting at time 200 and ending at time 150, or
gene flow starting at time 150 and ending at time 200.

Which of those two calls to gene_flow() do you think will result in an error and why?






NoteClick to see the solution





Programming gene flow starting at time 200 and ending at time 150 effectively implies a backward direction of time. This isn’t a problem, necessarily, except that the information about histories of pA and pC populations (actually, only the pC population! can you tell why?) makes slendr’s gene_flow() function enforce a forward direction of time.

gf <- gene_flow(from = pA, to = pC, proportion = 0.42, start = 200, end = 150)

Error:
! Inconsistent time direction implied by population and gene-flow timings


The second version works, of course, for the same reason:

gf <- gene_flow(from = pA, to = pC, proportion = 0.42, start = 150, end = 200)





Note: There are other cases in which even the enforcement of model consistency described above still allows broken models to be programmed, which is why compile_model() provides yet another set of sanity checks. But we will leave those aside for now. If you end up running into these issues, this exercise has already equipped you to understand why slendr sometimes gives errors and how to interpret them to fix your models.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Exercise: Resize events
Of course, populations in traditional demographic models in evolutionary and population genetics don’t just split and mix—they also experience population bottlenecks, population expansions, contractions, etc. The means to program these demographic events is through the function resize().
In slendr, these events come in two variants, which we can call step resizes or exponential resizes.

Step resizes

We can implement immediate step resize events simply by calling the function resize(), providing the new size N and the time at which the resize event should occur.

Exponential resizes

If we need to implement exponential resize event (either exponential increase or decrease of population size), we provide the new size N, the time at which the resizing should start (same as for step resizes) but also the time at which it should end. From this information, slendr is able to interpolate the resizes needed at each time point in order to simulate the gradual exponential change.

Practice the use of the resize() function by programming a bottleneck event in the history of the population p3 in your script slendr_models_human.qmd. The bottleneck should happen at 1800 years BP, with the population contracting to the size of 100 individuals. Then program the recovery of this population, resizing in a step-wise fashion to size of 2000 individual at time 1000 years BP. Use the function plot_model() to visualize your new model and validate that you’ve programmed the bottleneck scenario correctly (remember to call it by setting its argument proportion = TRUE).






NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 30,
  time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportion = TRUE)













Note: The visualization of the exponential is a bit wonky in that it makes things look like a gradual linear change—apologies for that! This will be fixed in a future slendr version.

title: Building slendr models
text:
Bonus exercise: Models on disk
Feel free to skip this exercise, unless you managed to run through everything quickly and want to learn a little bit about slendr internals. Especially if you’re a little bit familiar with msprime or SLiM, this might be quite interesting.
A very important part of slendr’s approach to modeling is to make simple things be trivially easy. This is largely why expressing even relatively complex models with slendr requires so little code compared to the amount of programming needed with traditional powerful simulators.
Still, sometimes it’s useful to peek behind the curtain and see what exactly is going on inside slendr and how it operates.

Type out the model object in the R console, paying attention to the description of the path where it’s been compiled. Use your operating system disk browsing program (Finder on macOS, File Explorer on Windows, or any other means of browsing files on other systems, such as the terminal shell) to see what files are hiding in that path. Given the model we’ve programmed so far, pay particular attention to populations.tsv and geneflow.tsv. What format do those files have? Can you decipher the meaning of the information they store by comparing it to your own model R code?

Both scripts are designed to read individual “model configuration files” (some of which we looked at right above) and use them to create a dedicated simulation run in either of the two “simulation engines” written in msprime or SLiM.

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Preparation
The exercises in this chapter will pick up from where we left of in the chapter on building slendr demographic models, and use this as a basis to learn how to simulate genomic data from these models.
To make sure we’re all on the same page, saving the following code in a new script slendr_scheduling.R. You can see that it’s basically the outcome of the exercises in the previous chapter on building demographic models with slendr.
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Exercise: Simulating genomic data
Once we have compiled a slendr model, we can finally simulate data from it. By default, a simulation from a slendr model always produces a tree-sequence object as a result. We’ll explore the tree-sequence concept in a bit more detail later—for now we can treat it as a black box which “magically” stores genomic variation of a set of individuals.
There are two simulation engines built into slendr implemented by functions msprime() and slim(). For traditional, non-spatial, neutral demographic models, the msprime() engine is much more efficient, so we’ll be using that for the time being.


Note: The alternative engine implemented by the slim() function plays an important role for spatial simulations and for simulations of natural selection — these are the primary two reasons why it’s included in slendr in the first place.
As we discussed in the introduction, here’s how you can use simulate a tree sequence from a compiled slendr model. You will be seeing this kind of pattern over and over again, so it’s worth keeping it in mind any time you will be simulating data going forward.

ts <- msprime(
  model,
  sequence_length = <length of the simulated genome [in bp]>,
  recombination_rate = <uniform recombination rate [in crossovers per bp per generation]>
)


Simulate a tree sequence from your compiled model by adding the appropriate msprime() command into the script slendr_scheduling.R, storing it in a variable ts. Set the parameters sequence_length = 1e6 and recombination_rate = 1e-8.






NoteClick to see the solution





This command simulates a tskit tree sequence from a slendr model. Again, note that we don’t have to write any msprime or tskit code to implement the simulation because slendr does all the work for us!

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)





Now type out the ts object in the console — what do you see? Try to relate some of the information in the presented summary to our overview discussion of tree sequences. For instance, what are the “nodes” and “edges”? What’s the difference between “samples” and “individuals”? How many “trees” does the tree sequence have, and how many “mutations” are stored in it?






NoteClick to see the solution

For instance, our tree sequence contains genomic information for 5000, each of them diploid. This makes for 10000 samples in total, where a “sample” is a “node” in a tree sequence representing one haplotype (i.e., one chromosome) of a simulated individual. All other “nodes” (of which there are many, many more) represent ancestral haplotypes of these recorded individuals for which we generally have only a part of their genomic information—a sequence information which made it through recombination to some of the recorded samples.
And notice that there are no mutations! How can this be possible, if we supposedly ran a genomic simulation? More on that later!





Note: Similarly to the symbol model, whenever we from now on refer to ts, we will be talking about some simulated tree-sequence object stored in an R variable ts.

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Exercise: Referring to simulated individuals
If we are to use tree-sequence data for computation of population genomic statistics, we need a way to refer to individuals and populations. For this purpose, slendr provides three important functions: ts_recorded(), ts_names(), and (sometimes, but not often, also useful) ts_nodes(). At the bare minimum, these functions accept the tree sequence ts as their first argument (i.e., can be run such as ts_recorded(ts)).

Try answering these questions by running these three functions and inspecting and comparing their outputs:

How many individuals are in your tree sequence based on these functions?
How is the result of ts_nodes() different from ts_recorded()?
What are the time values of recorded individuals based on the information produced by these two functions? Are the time values the same in both?
How many individuals in total are in the tree sequence based on these two functions, and how many of them are in each population? Why do you get the numbers you got, given the model which you programmed and simulated?
How does ts_names() differ from the two table-producing functions?

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Exercise: Customizing sample recording
We can see that our tree sequence contains a massive number of individuals. Too many, in fact — we recorded every single individual alive at the end of our simulation, which is something we’re unlikely to be ever lucky enough to have, regardless of which species we study.
To get closer to the scale of the genomic data that we usually work with, we can restrict our simulation to only record a subset of individuals—we do this using a process called “scheduling of recorded individuals” implemented by the slendr function schedule_recording(). Simply speaking, this is a functionality of slendr which precisely defines which individuals will be recorded in the tree sequence while ignoring everyone else.
The function follows the structure in the following snippet, representing another very useful pattern worth keeping in mind going forward:

schedule <- schedule_recording(
  <compiled slendr model>,
  times = <times of recording>,
  list(<population object>, <number of samples to record>),
  [... etc. ... ]
)

We then use this schedule object in a standard msprime() function call, setting it as the argument of the same name (schedule =) like this:

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)


To get an idea about what this function does in practice, modify the command which simulates the ts object in your script slendr_scheduling.R according to the snippet above, but include a schedule for recording 5 individuals from each of the four populations. When you re-run the new simulation to get a new ts object and type ts into your console, do you see a change? Again, use your knowledge of ts_recorded() and some dplyr table processing function to inspect the recorded individuals.
Hint: To make this easier to see, maybe keep the original simulation command in your script (the one without the schedule) but modify it to create a variable ts_big instead before you create the new ts object.






NoteClick to see the solution






schedule <- schedule_recording(
  model,
  times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 5), list(p4, 5)
)

# original simulation command (note the missing schedule)
ts_big <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

# new (smaller) tree-sequence recording
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)

# see that the new tree sequence is much smaller (even its memory footprint)
ts

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Exercise: Complex recording schedules
What if we need to simulate different number of individuals from different populations at very specific times? Doing this with a single call to schedule_recording() is not possible. Luckily, multiple schedules can be easily combined together into a single sampling schedule.

Type the schedule variable in your R console. What do you see? Why did I say that multiple schedules can be easily combined? And how could we combine them?






NoteClick to see the solution





The output of any schedule_recording() function is a plain old data frame! It contains a bunch of information we used in the schedule_recording() call (population names, times, etc.), plus a bunch more additional data which is currently irrelevant. For instance, notice the time, pop, and n columns below:

schedule

# A tibble: 4 × 8
   time pop       n name  y_orig x_orig y     x    
  <int> <chr> <int> <lgl> <lgl>  <lgl>  <lgl> <lgl>
1     0 p1        5 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   
2     0 p2        5 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   
3     0 p3        5 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   
4     0 p4        5 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   





Normally we don’t ever have to look at this data (unless something goes wrong with the sampling and troubleshooting slendr itself is needed), but knowing the format of the schedule means we can easily combine multiple schedules using standard functions such as rbind() (included in base R).

In the following chapters, we will be working on implementing many real-world scenarios from widely established research in population genomics, particularly those from the field ancient DNA field. Naturally, in cases like this, we need to be able to simulate sequences of “ancient” individuals as well as various “present-day” reference panels.
In preparation for these complex exercises, implement the recording schedule summarized into the table below. You will have to figure out how many individual schedules you’ll have to create using schedule_recording(), then bind them together using the function rbind() mentioned above. Then, simulate a tree sequence ts with this new complex schedule, modifying your current solution script accordingly.

Hint: You can provide a vector of numbers as the times = argument of schedule_recording(). See the help page for ?schedule_recording for more information and to see a concrete example.






NoteClick to see the solution





Inspecting the table above, it looks like we have effectively two groups of recording events determined by the times indicated in the first column: one group of individuals in the “present-day” (i.e., at time 0) and a time-series of ancient individuals. So let’s leverage that to create two recording schedules, “modern” and “ancient”:
Scheduling of modern individuals:

modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p2, 1), list(p4, 10))
modern

# A tibble: 3 × 8
   time pop       n name  y_orig x_orig y     x    
  <int> <chr> <int> <lgl> <lgl>  <lgl>  <lgl> <lgl>
1     0 p1        1 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   
2     0 p2        1 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   
3     0 p4       10 NA    NA     NA     NA    NA   


Scheduling of ancient individuals:

ancient_times <- seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000)
ancient_times

[1] 5000 4000 3000 2000 1000

ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = ancient_times, list(p3, 5))

We can then create a single sampling schedulie like this:

schedule <- rbind(modern, ancient)

And use it in our simulation just like we showed above:

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)

Let’s verify that we got the correct number of individuals:

ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop, time) %>% tally

# A tibble: 8 × 3
# Groups:   pop [4]
  pop    time     n
  <chr> <dbl> <int>
1 p1        0     1
2 p2        0     1
3 p3     1000     5
4 p3     2000     5
5 p3     3000     5
6 p3     4000     5
7 p3     5000     5
8 p4        0    10

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Exercise: Recording of named individuals
Sometimes, we don’t just want to record a given set of “anonymous” individuals, but we want to be able to work with unique, named individuals. This can be especially helpful when we want to reconstruct a particular scenario in some specific archaeological context (for instance, we want to work with some very precious archaeological sample, such as the “Altai Neanderthal”).
We can do so by calling schedule_recording() in a slightly modified way which doesn’t use the normal syntax list(<population>, <number>), to record a given number of individuals from the given population, but instead uses the format of list(<population>, 1, "<name of the individual>").

Use this format to modify your recording schedule (for instance, based on combining two recording schedules called modern and ancient) to implement a unique recording event which will give the one representative individual of the admixture source population the name "source_ind" and the outgroup individual will be named "outgroup_ind". Then create a new combined schedule again, and verify that you got the newly named individuals in a new simulated tree sequence ts.






NoteClick to see the solution





We’ll be more succinct now (see the full explanation to the modern and ancient schedules in the solution to the previous exercise):

outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source<- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)

Now we can simulate a new tree sequence with more specifically named individuals:

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)

And verify that we did everything correctly by inspecting the table of the contents of the tree sequence:

ts_recorded(ts) %>% print(n = Inf)

You may have noticed that plot_model() has a number of optional arguments. One of them is called schedule and it accepts a sampling schedule (such as the one you just created) as its input. Use your model and sampling schedule to visualize your model.
This functionality can be useful as an additional validation of your modeling scripts, so always remember to use this for sanity checking your simulations (after all, a picture can be worth more than thousand words dozens of lines of code)!






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s is the model on its own:

plot_model(model)








Here is the model with sampling numbers overlaid on top:

Note: As you’ve seen above, the visualization is often a bit wonky and convoluted with overlapping elements, so don’t be too frustrated if the results of your plot_model() visualizations are not too pretty. The function has been designed as a validation and troubleshooting tool, rather than a tool to create publication-ready figures.

title: Simulating genomic data
text:
Catch up
If you want to just catch up to the point at which this section would conclude, here is the version of our simulation script at the end of the final exercise:






NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 10000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 2000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 5000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 2000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source<- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)








ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Preparation
Computing population genetic statistics requires a specification of what should be computed and how. Which individuals should a computation be performed on? If multiple individuals should be grouped together, how do we define these groups?
This chapter will teach you how to do this with slendr by guiding you through exercises focused on the most fundamental concepts of population genomics. The focus will be less on teaching you how these concepts work (after all, you might be already be quite familiar with population genetics from your studies or work) and more to give you the opportunity to learn the technicalities of R and slendr in a familiar context.
That said, I have designed the exercises to provide interesting puzzles to showcase the usefulness of simulation-based exploration even in (seemingly) basic scenarios and applications, so that even readers relatively well familiar with population genomics will appreciate a new perspective on familiar topics. Every single one of them represents a question I myself had, and my solutions are the means I used myself to get the answers.
Let’s start with the following single-population model to keep things as simple as possible. Look through the code to understand what it does, then save it as slendr_statistics.R. Run the entire script and inspect the produced visualization to make sure your understanding is correct.
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)

model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

plot_model(model)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

samples <- ts_names(ts)

ts <-
