title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Within-group(s) statistics — nucleotide diversity
The simplest possible computation we can do is to compute a statistic from a single population. As an example, let’s look at nucleotide diversity \(\pi\), implemented by a slendr function ts_diversity().
If you look at its help page under ?ts_diversity, you will see that it accepts several arguments—for now let’s focus on the first two, ts = (which is obviously a tree-sequence object, such as the one produced by the msprime() engine) and sample_sets =.

Compute ts_diversity() on a single simulated individual, such as the individual with the name “pop_1”. Knowing that slendr simulates diploids and knowing the definition of nucleotide diversity, how would you interpret the result?






NoteClick to see the solution





The answer is that we get that individual’s heterozygosity—the proportion of their genome (two chromosomes, because each individual is diploid) carrying heterozygous sites:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 pop_1  0.000173





Note that this is the same thing as the following command:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1"))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 pop_1  0.000173


This is because in R, a single value is the same thing as a vector of length one (this might seem like a bit of curious R trivia but it’s good to keep in mind):

"single_value" == c("single_value")

[1] TRUE

length(c("single_value"))

[1] 1

length("single_value")

[1] 1






Now run the following three commands. They look extremely similar, right? Do they produce the same value? If not, can you decipher a general rule from the results obtained how slendr interprets these?

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))

It turns out that patterns like these are very important for computing any kind of tree-sequence statistic with slendr, so it very much pays off to think about this, even though this looks trivial and nit-picky!






NoteClick to see the solution





The first command is supposed to demonstrate that specifying a vector of individuals’ names to a statistic which operates within a given group of samples simply computes that statistic as if each individual was its own sample:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 pop_1  0.000173
2 pop_2  0.000222


The second command features the same vector of names, but wrapped in list(). This is how you can instruct slendr to treat a given set of individuals as a group—and in this case, compute a statistic for the group as a whole. In this context, this command computes the nucleotide diversity within the given sample of two individuals from the whole population “pop”:

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 set_1  0.000200


Notice that slendr assigned this “anonymous” group of individuals the name “set_1”. Because these default names can be confusing in more complex computations of more complex statistics, you can optionally specify the name of your group by providing the set of individuals as a named list instead (see the R bootcamp chapter in case you need a refresher on named lists and similar topics):

ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set        diversity
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 pop_subset  0.000200






Of course, you can compute any statistic not only for one group of individuals, but for multiple of them. What result such computation produces depends on whether we’re computing so-called “one-way” statistics (which are computed within groups, like nucleotide diversity here) or “multi-way” statistic (which are computed between groups, like \(F_{ST}\)). For now we’ll stay with one-way statistics.
To make the “one-way” statistic concept clear, let’s practice this. Instead of computing ts_diversity() for a single group of individuals (like “pop_1” and “pop_2” above), compute this using a single ts_diversity() command on multiple subsets of individuals of increasing sizes (let’s say groups of 1, 2, 5, 10, 500 1000, and finally all individuals). Do you expect the same value of nucleotide diversity? And why?
Hint: You can get a random subset of a larger set of elements using the built-in R function sample(). Take a look at ?sample manual page if you need more help.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s first generate the subsets of individuals of different sizes. We have a number of options:

We could do it “manually” like this:


# first get all names of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence
all_inds <- ts_names(ts)

# then manually create all subset names
subsets <- list(
  sample(all_inds, 1),
  sample(all_inds, 2),
  sample(all_inds, 5),
  sample(all_inds, 10),
  sample(all_inds, 500),
  sample(all_inds, 1000),
  all_inds
)


Alternatively, we could do it more succinctly using this R pattern:


# first get the desired sizes of all subsets
sizes <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 500, 1000, length(all_inds))

# then iterate over those sizes, and applying the sample() function to each
subsets <- lapply(sizes, sample, x = all_inds)
# let's also add names to the groups based on their sizes, for easier reference
names(subsets) <- sizes

Either way, these commands give us a list of vector of appropriate lengths, which we can verify like this. It’s very useful to do these sanity checks as your working on your programs, always making sure that what you want to do actually matches reality:

# apple the length() function to each element of the list
sapply(subsets, length)

   1    2    5   10  500 1000 5000 
   1    2    5   10  500 1000 5000 


Now we can finally compute nucleotide diversity in each of those groups of individuals:

ts_diversity(ts, subsets)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 1      0.000192
2 2      0.000189
3 5      0.000191
4 10     0.000198
5 500    0.000197
6 1000   0.000197
7 5000   0.000197


Perhaps not surprisingly, we don’t see much difference. After all, this is expected, because there is only one true (and normally unknown) value of nucleotide diversity of the entire population. What changes when we compute this statistic on subsets of different sizes is the stochastic noise.
We’ll see a bit more on how to control (and quantify) the noise using simulations a little bit later.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Parameter estimation — \(N_e\)
In practical research, we often use various software or statistics to estimate some parameter of interest. In our context—again, to use a very simple toy example to demonstrate a simulation-based approach in a familiar context—let’s look at a measure of the population size called effective population size, or \(N_e\).
From a bit of background theory of population genetics, we know that we can obtain an estimate of \(N_e\) from nucleotide diversity (which we just computed). Specifically, neutral theory of molecular evolution posits that an idealised diploid population will have a pairwise nucleotide diversity equal to
\[\theta = 4 N_e \mu,\]
where \(\mu\) is the mutation rate. Using simple algebra to rearrange this equation, this gives us an estimate for \(N_e\) in the form of
\[N_e = \frac{\theta}{4 \mu}.\]
Let’s build a simple simulation-based analysis to determine how well does this estimator perform under different scenarios.


If you’re familiar with population genetics, this has all sorts of obvious answers, but let’s demonstrate how we can benchmark this using simulations, hopefully establishing a useful slendr recipe which you will be able to use very often in all kinds of contexts (some of the more complex ones will be demonstrated later in this workshop).

Start by computing the nucleotide diversity value for every single individual in your tree sequence and storing the result in a data frame df. Then, use the equation above to estimate \(N_e\) from nucleotide diversity, and add a new column Ne_estimated to this data frame with this value. Do you get a reasonable result?
Hint: Remember that you know the true \(N_e\) in your model — it’s the N value in your simulation script! That’s the most powerful thing about simulations — they allow you to establish a ground truth, and benchmark various methods against it!






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s get the data frame with the value of \(\pi\) first:

df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
df

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  set   diversity
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 all    0.000197


Then add the inferred \(N_e\) according to the equation above:

df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
df

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  set   diversity Ne_estimated
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>
1 all    0.000197        4927.





Of course, benchmarking any method based on a single simulation of a single number doesn’t make sense — so now let’s now take things one step forward.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Generalizing the simulation
Suppose we need to evaluate how our hypothetical statistic of interest (in this example, the estimator of \(N_e\)) behaves under different parameters, different, models, different bioinformatic processing, etc.
To do this, we could make a copy of our original script, modify it a bunch of times, and re-run the modifications as needed, collecting the results in the process. This works, but is almost always the wrong approach. The correct way to do this is to generalize our code into a self-contained function.
To demonstrate, let’s break this down into individual steps (in software engineering, this process of modifying code and improving it is called “refactoring”).

First, create and save a new script called slendr_Ne_pi.R. We’ll be working on our improvements in this new file.

In this script, create a function called sim_constant, which will accept a single argument Ne_true, and will “wrap around” the following bits of code (in other words, copy-pasting what you programmed in the original slendr_statistics.R and wrapping it into a function):

the code implementing our slendr demographic model,
the command simulating a ts object from the model,
the commands creating the df data frame with nucleotide diversity,
the computation of Ne_estimated from nucleotide diversity,
adding a column to df called Ne_true and assigning it the Ne_true argument of your function.
Your function should return this df object as its output.

When you’re done, all the code doing the above should be gone from your script, entirely replaced by this function.
Hint: If you need help, you can use the following template which shows how should your script look like when you’re done.

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(model) {
  # move the bits of code doing 1.-6. inside this function

  # write the bits of code to do 5. and 6. afterwards

  # finally, return the df data frame like this
  return(df)
}







NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s how my entire slendr_statistics_Ne.R looks like:

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}





To test your function, restart your R session (in RStudio go to Session -> Restart R), then run your entire script. Then, evaluate your function in the R console by running it for different values of \(N_e\) (for instance, type sim_constant(100), sim_constant(1234),sim_constant(20000)`, etc.). Each of your function calls should produce a data frame with the appropriate value of \(\pi\) and the estimated \(N_e\).






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s what I get with my implementation:

sim_constant(Ne_true = 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set    diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>      <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all   0.00000479         120.     100

sim_constant(Ne_true = 1234)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set   diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all   0.0000538        1346.    1234

sim_constant(Ne_true = 20000)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  set   diversity Ne_estimated Ne_true
  <chr>     <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 all    0.000745       18636.   20000






Doing all this extra programming work might seem like unnecessary bother. In fact, it looks like we’ve so far written even more code! But the pay off comes later, as you will see.
Custom functions are absolutely critical for efficient, reproducible science. They eliminate copy-pasted bug-prone code and make it much easier to explore ideas, test parameters, and explore various models. In this workshop, I’ll be often forcing you to write custom functions—hopefully, by the end you will appreciate why I did this!

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Simulations across parameter grids
Whenever we want to benchmark a statistic, or understand its expected behavior under different circumstances, we often need to re-run a model many times, usually for different model parameters (or different models entirely).
Imagine we want to compute our inference on many different potential values of true \(N_e\), what we could do is something like the exercise above, running the model individually. But this isn’t very scalable, definitely whenever we want to run the same model across a huge number of parameter values (or even multiple such parameters).
In cases like this, we want to is to use “looping”, such as the function map_dfr() from the package purrr:
Imagine a function like this, which creates a data frame of a value and its square:

silly_fun <- function(x) {
  data.frame(value = x, squared = x * x)
}

The way we use map_dfr is by providing a list of values of our parameter of interest, and a function name. In the case of our silly function, we can use it like this:

library(purrr)

map_dfr(c(100, 1234, 20000), silly_fun)

  value   squared
1   100     10000
2  1234   1522756
3 20000 400000000


The name map_dfr stands for _“map a given function producing a data frame and then bind its rows together, hence, map_dfr. When you look at its output above, this is exactly what happened.

In your script slendr_statistics_Ne.R, program a simulation of \(N_e\) inference across the grid of Ne_true values of c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000), then visualize the results as a scatterplot of Ne_true against Ne_estimated. Use the function purrr::map_dfr() to do this efficiently.






NoteClick to see the solution






library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)

ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")












This toy exercise is a great example of how to use these kinds of simulations in practice. Again, nucleotide diverisity-based \(N_e\) estimation and its benchmarking across a range of parameters really is a toy example, but this idea extends to many other settings:

benchmarking of IBD accuracy across different gene-flow scenarios
validating qpAdm inference results for various possible admixture graphs
testing the robustness of local ancestry inference methods (LAI) and admixture dating inference as a function of admixture times and proportions
understanding how PCA differs for different sample sizes from different populations

… and many others. All of this is something that I do in my daily work (and something that almost any paper in population genomics should be doing to validate their results).

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Comparing multiple models
Let’s make it a bit more interesting. Suppose we want to see how robust our statistic of interest is to the underlying demographic model (which is almost always uncertain).
In the previous exercise, we worked with using \(\pi\) to estimate the \(N_e\) a population under study (\(N_e\)) and verified that it works very well for a model of a long-term constant population size.
But what about population that experienced a resize event? How well does our \(N_e\) estimate work in such case?

In your script slendr_statistics_Ne.R, make a copy of your function sim_constant() named sim_resize(). Make the following changes in this function:

the population “pop” will start with \(N_e\) of 5000,
the population will experience a population resize (implemented by the function resize()), which will set the size of the population to the function argument Ne_true at time 500.

Then, use the function map_dfr() to run the new function sim_resize() along the same parameter grid as before, again visualizing the results of Ne_true against Ne_estimated. How well does our diversity-based \(N_e\) estimate perform in such a demographic scenario? Is it robust to non-constant demographic histories? If not, why?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the solution—new function sim_resize(), new simulation run against a parameter grid, and a visualization of results:

# new function to simulate population size change
sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# simulations across a parameter grid
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)

# visualization of results
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









We can see that even a large population resize event doesn’t change the observed levels of nucleotide diversity that much. As a result, the \(N_e\) based on the population nucleotide diversity parameter \(\theta\) is very wrong—we consistently estimate it at the level of 5000 (i.e., the size prior to the bottleneck), regardless of the true size of the population after the bottleneck.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Expanding the parameter grid
Our hypothesis for how poorly the nucleotide diversity-based estimate is doing under non-constant population size is the fact that the resize event was very recent. As a result, diversity hasn’t yet reached an equilibrium value.
Let’s test this hypothesis while, at the same time, showing how we can expand the parameter grid simulations to include another parameter—this time the time of the population size change.






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the solution.
First, the new function sim_resize()

sim_change <- function(Ne_true, T_change) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = T_change)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  df$T_change <- T_change
  
  df
}

A new simulation run against a parameter grid:

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- rbind(
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1),    # change 1 generation ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100),  # change 100 generations ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1000), # etc.
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 2000)
)

And finally, visualization of results:

ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)",
          subtitle = "Each panel indicates the time of the population size change") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000) +
  facet_wrap(~ T_change)

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









We can see that, indeed, the older the population resize event, the more time there’s for the population to either lose the variation (in case of a bottleneck), or gain new variation (in case of population size increase), which means that the \(N_e\) estimated based on the \(\theta = 4 N_e \mu\) nucleotide diversity parameter is going to be close to the true (unknown) population size.




In the case of this example, the problem with the nucleotide diversity is that it effectively reduces the entirety of genetic variation in the population (which mutations there are at which frequencies) into a single number. As a result, we lose a lot of potentially very useful information about the population’s demographic history. When we try to estimate \(N_e\) using this summary statistic, we can only hope to infer a long-term \(N_e\).
As we’ve seen, a single bottleneck doesn’t cause nucleotide diversity to drop significantly enough for us to pick up that this bottleneck even happened.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Allele frequency spectrum (AFS)
Create a new script called slendr_Ne_afs.R. Copy-paste the following code into that script. Note that this is the same exact model we started this section (except for the one line which selects only 20 individuals from all individuals recorded in the tree sequence).

library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)
model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)


Unlike nucleotide diversity which, as mentioned above, reduces the entire genomic variation of a population into a single number, the allele frequency spectrum carries information about the distribution of the counts of mutations at each observable frequency.
Look at the ?ts_afs help page to learn how the slendr function ts_afs() works. As you’ve seen, ts_diversity() (like the vast majority of slendr statistical functions) produces a data frame. What data format does ts_afs() produce? Compute the AFS from your simulated tree sequence ts on your subset of individuals, then visualize it (with whatever means you know).






NoteClick to see the solution





As we can see, ts_afs() produces a plain R vector of integer numbers, each of which represents the count of mutations observed at a given frequency — the count of singletons, the count of doubletons, etc.:

afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
afs

 [1] 1214  197  102   82   53   31   20   37   21   12   16    4   11   23   12
[16]   10   13   11    9   10   10


This vector can be easily visualized with a base-R function plot():

plot(afs, type = "l", col = "lightblue", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")












But does the AFS really carry more information about demographic changes?
Write a new function in your script, called sim_afs(), which will again accept a single argument Ne_true and implement the exact same demographic model as you did in your function sim_change() (i.e., resize from the initial N of 5000 to the given value of Ne_true at time 1000). In this function, compute the afs vector from this model, then run it for a range of Ne_true values and visualize the individual AFS results. Does AFS pick up signal even from such recent population size changes?






NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s a function which simulates an AFS for a demographic history given by the Ne_true argument:

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)

  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}


df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)


ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")








For easier comparison, here are the AFS result side-by-side with the values of nucleotide diversity from the same demographic scenarios:


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









This simulation indicates that AFS does, indeed, carry much more information about population history, even for recent changes in population size.




For now we’ll leave this topic be. We could go much deeper into this, but the point of this chapter was to demonstrate how to compute within-population statistics with slendr, how we can use manipulation of R lists and vectors to instruct slendr on how to compute a given statistic, and provide a set of small examples of how population genomic simulations (even extremely simple ones!) and a bit of data processing can be used to build intuition into sometimes unintuitive concepts.
Towards the end of the workshop, we’re going to work through a slightly more realistic case-study which will demonstrate how to do simulation-based inference by extending our toy example of \(N_e\) estimation towards a more real-world scenario.
For now, we’re going to move on into computing between-group statistics and use similar computational methodology to explore a couple of concepts behind metrics such as \(F_{ST}\) or \(f\)-statistics.

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Catch up
Here is a complete solution to the exercises in this section represented by a single tidy reproducible R script:






NoteClick to see the entire script





For simplicity, this script only evaluates models when the size change happens 1000 generations ago (but it could be expanded, of course).

# first we import a couple of packages ------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

# function which simulates a constant size model --------------------------

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates a model of population size change --------------

sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates the AFS from a size change model ---------------

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}

# run simulations across a given grid -------------------------------------

# for the constant model, these values represent the constant Ne, for the size
# change model they represent the final Ne after the initial size of 5000

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)
df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)
df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)

# visualize the results ---------------------------------------------------

# diversity in the constant size models
ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")







ggsave("constant_size_pi.pdf")

Saving 7 x 5 in image

# diversity in the size change models
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'








ggsave("changing_size_pi.pdf")

Saving 7 x 5 in image
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'

# AFS in the size change models
ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")







ggsave("changing_size_afs.pdf")

Saving 7 x 5 in image

title: Within-population statistics
text:
Bonus exercise: Your own model
If you got all the way here while the others are still working on their solutions, here’s a bonus exercise for you.
Take a demographic model of an organism or a population which is of your interest in your own research (either your own model or a model you know from the literature) and program it with slendr. Feel free to be as detailed (or not) as possible, but don’t worry about accuracy of various parameters. The point is to practice building a model from scratch. Then, compute the basic summary statistics introduced in this chapter on simulations from your model. Do the results match what you know, either from your research or from the literature? If not, what could be the problem?
If these statistics aren’t particularly interesting or relevant for your research, don’t despair. Again, the point is to practice, but even then, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to compute more interesting things throughout this course, particularly during the “freeform” sessions at the very end.

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Exercise: Recap on R lists and vectors
In the previous session, you learned to compute within-group summary statistics by providing slendr functions single vectors of individual names, most easily obtained by the function ts_names() in a very straightforward way.
Whenever we work with “between-group statistics” (i.e., statistics based on comparing genomic variation between different groupings of individuals), we need to be aware of some of the ways of how R works with lists and vectors. This is not difficult, but it is something that doesn’t come up in daily work in R in a normal data analysis setting.
Let’s first set up a small model to demonstrate this.
Start by creating a new R script called slendr-multipop.R and program the following model in it, simulating a tree sequence object ts (sequence length 10Mb, recombination rate 1e-8, mutation rate 1e-8). In this tree sequence, schedule the recording of ten individuals from each of the three populations at time 0 (i.e., the “present-day”).
Hint: Note that unlike our previous toy examples, this model features multiple populations, so you will need to program population splits. Remember that you can specify that a population should split from some parent lineage by using the population(..., parent = <parent population object>) format.
Now let’s work on a couple of basic vector- and list-based operations in R, which we will be using all the time. If you need a recap, you can scroll through the introductory R bootcamp chapter, particularly sections and exercises relevant for subsetting and indexing into vectors and lists in R.
You’re already familiar with the calling the function ts_names() as ts_names(ts). Add this command to your script, saving its result as samples. What is the type of the data stored in the samples variable? What does this information tell us and how is it different from running simply ts_names(ts)?
Using R list manipulation, how do you access the names of individuals in the population X? What’s the difference between calling samples$X, samples[["X"]], and samples["X"]?
(This might seem extremely trivial and boring, but is very important for R programming in general and for correct computation of population genetic statistics with slendr. So bear with me please!)
OK, so why does this matter?
Remember how in the previous chapter, you sometimes needed to indicate a named sample of some individuals in a slightly convoluted way in order to compute a statistic on all of them, such as:
list(group_name = c("X_1", "X_2", "X_3"))

$group_name
[1] "X_1" "X_2" "X_3"
Doing so for complex computations is very annoying. But also—notice how the chunk above produces the exact same format as samples["X"] earlier. This is why I implemented the variant ts_names(ts, split = TRUE) in slendr, as a shortcut. As you’ll se below, this makes it possible to use the samples variable to instruct slendr to perform computation very efficiently.

title: Between-population statistics
text:
NoteClick to see the solution






library(slendr)
init_env()

outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
X <- population("X", N = 1000, time = 3000, parent = outgroup)
Y <- population("Y", N = 1000, time = 3000, parent = outgroup)

model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

plot_model(model, order = c("outgroup", "X", "Y"), proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)







ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)













NoteClick to see the solution





The command ts_names(ts) produces vector of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence:

samples <- ts_names(ts)
class(samples)

[1] "character"


The variation ts_names(ts, split = TRUE) gives us a (named!) list of vectors, one for each population.

samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
class(samples)

[1] "list"














NoteClick to see the solution





The first extracts a separate vector of X individuals from the list:

samples$X

 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"


The same goes for this variant:

samples[["X"]]

 [1] "X_1"  "X_2"  "X_3"  "X_4"  "X_5"  "X_6"  "X_7"  "X_8"  "X_9"  "X_10"


The third is very different. It looks the same, but it’s actually a list with a single element (the vector of names)!

samples["X"]

$X

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Exercise: “Outgroup” \(f_3\) statistic


Note: The \(f_3\) statistic is traditionally expressed as \(f_3(A, B; C)\), where C represents the outgroup. Unfortunately, in tskit the outgroup is named A, with B and C being the pair of samples from which we trace the length of branches towards the outgroup, so the statistic is interpreted as \(f_3(B, C;
A).\)

Create a new script split_simulation.R and paste your three-population simulation code from slendr-multipop.Ri n it. We’ll be continuing our work in this new script, starting with two modifications:

First, wrap the code in a function called simulate_split(). This function should accept a single argument tsplit which will parametrize at which point should “X” and “Y” populations split from the “outgroup” lineage.
Then, compute the outgroup \(f_3\) statistic using the function ts_f3(), setting the B = argument to the “X” individuals, C = argument to the “Y” individuals, and the C = argument to the “outgroup” individuals (remember to use the samples variable produced by the ts_names() shortcut above).
The function should return a data frame produced by the ts_f3() function, with a new column named tsplit containing the value of this function argument.







NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s the content of the script split_simulation.R:

library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_split <- function(tsplit) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = 1000, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = 1000, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))
  
  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
  df <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  
  return(df)
}





Test your function simulate_split() by calling it on a few split times in the R console (like 1000, 2000, or 5000 generations). Then, use your well-known function map_dfr() from the purrr package to compute it on a grid of split times between 1 and 10000 generations in steps of every 1000 generations. Visualize the statistical expectation of the \(f_3\) statistic in a scatterplot as a function of the split time. Add all this code in your script split_simulation.R after your function definition.






NoteClick to see the solution





Let’s test the function first:

title: Between-population statistics
section: Exercise: Statistical power of \(F_{ST}\) vs outgroup \(f_3\)
text:
Exercise: Statistical power of \(F_{ST}\) vs outgroup \(f_3\)
Another statistic which is very frequently used as a measure of population differentiation is [\(F_{ST}](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixation_index).
Let's say we want to understand, which of the two (\)f_3$ or $F_{ST}) is more robust to \(N_e\) differences between the two populations under study. Recall that \(N_e\) determines the amount of genetic drift (and, therefore, the rate of the loss) of genomic variation in a population. In other words, if you were interested in measuring how far in the past the populations began differentiating, would both of them give you a reliable answer, regardless of the \(N_e\) of those populations?
Both \(F_{ST}\) and \(f_3\) are routinely used as measures of population differentiation—can we use them equivalently? Does one have potentially more statistical power than the other?

We want to evaluate the impact of \(N_e\), so let’s modify our function simulate_split() a little bit first:

Right now the function accepts a single argument tsplit. Add a second argument to this function called Ne, then modify the two lines of code indicating splits of “X” and “Y” population and change the fixed values of 1000 to use the new flexible parameters Ne.
Modify the function so that it returns in the resulting data frame not only the \(f_3\) value (computed by ts_f3()) but also the \(F_{ST}\) value (computed by ts_fst()). Look up the help for ?ts_fst to see how to use it (it’s very similar to using the ts_f3() function).
In the original function, you added a tsplit column to the data frame, to be able to know which f3 value corresponds to which tsplit parameter. In the new function, add another column Ne serving the same purpose.







NoteClick to see the solution





Here’s how the modified function looks like:

simulate_split <- function(tsplit, Ne) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 25))
  
  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
  value_fst <- ts_fst(ts, sample_sets = samples[c("X", "Y")])$Fst
  value_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])$f3

  df <- data.frame(statistic = c("Fst", "f3"), value = c(value_fst, value_f3))
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  df$Ne <- Ne
  
  return(df)
}

And here’s how we can check that it works:

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 100)

  statistic        value tsplit  Ne
1       Fst 9.229238e-01   3000 100
2        f3 3.740873e-05   3000 100

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 1000)

  statistic        value tsplit   Ne
1       Fst 4.259840e-01   3000 1000
2        f3 3.335793e-05   3000 1000

simulate_split(tsplit = 3000, Ne = 5000)

  statistic        value tsplit   Ne
1       Fst 9.989458e-02   3000 5000
2        f3 3.048318e-05   3000 5000






You’re already familiar with the basics of working with the iteration looping function map_dfr(). Use this function to run a new batch of parameter grid simulations, this time fixing the parameter tsplit = 3000, and only simulating the model for the values of the \(N_e\) parameter indicated below.
Hint: You can use the function map_dfr() to iterate over a given vector of values intended for only one of its function arguments (here Ne) while also explicitly setting its other argument(s) to a single fixed value—this is useful in cases in which we want to investigate only one parameter of interest while ignoring the others.**
Because this might seem a bit complicated, you can use this code to run the new grid simulations using your modified function simulate_split().

Ne_grid <- c(100, seq(from = 1000, to = 10000, by = 1000))
Ne_grid

 [1]   100  1000  2000  3000  4000  5000  6000  7000  8000  9000 10000

# run `simulate_split()` for each of the `Ne_grid` values, and set the second
# argument of the function to a fixed value `tsplit = 3000`
df <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_split, tsplit = 3000)

When you’re done, visualize the expected values of f3 and Fst summary statistics as functions of \(N_e\)and, therefore, their robustness to genetic drift—which one of them will be more reliable?






NoteClick to see the solution






ggplot(df, aes(Ne, value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("Fst and f3 for X-Y split at 3000 generations ago, assuming given Ne")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Conclusion: unlike \(F_{ST}\), the \(f_3\) statistic really is an unbiased estimator of population divergence with respect to \(N_e\) of the two lineages!

Here is a complete solution to the exercises so far, represented by a single tidy reproducible R script split_simulation.R.

library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)

library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# this is the second version of the function simulate_split() which accepts
# both tsplit and Ne as function arguments
simulate_split <- function(tsplit, Ne) {
  # set up the three-population demographic model
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 1000, time = 10000)
  X <- population("X", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  Y <- population("Y", N = Ne, time = tsplit, parent = outgroup)
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, X, Y), generation_time = 1)
  
  # simulate a tree sequence which will record a defined set of 25 individuals
  # from each population at the end of the simulation (i.e., "present-day")
  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 25))
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # extract the list of names of individuals in each population for convenience
  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
  # compute both summary statistics and extract their values as single numbers
  value_fst <- ts_fst(ts, sample_sets = samples[c("X", "Y")])$Fst
  value_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = samples["outgroup"], B = samples["X"], C = samples["Y"])$f3

  # construct a data frame with all the necessary information
  df <- data.frame(statistic = c("Fst", "f3"), value = c(value_fst, value_f3))
  df$tsplit <- tsplit
  df$Ne <- Ne
  
  return(df)
}


# this is the original exploration of f3 as a function of split time, slightly
# tweaked to use the version of simulate_split() parametrizable by both
# tsplit and Ne (recall that the first version used only the tsplit argument)
f3_outgroup <- map_dfr(seq(1, 10000, by = 1000), simulate_split, Ne = 1000)

# and visualization of the results
f3_outgroup %>%
filter(statistic == "f3", Ne == 1000) %>%
ggplot(aes(tsplit, value)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10000))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








# this is the comparison of the statistical power of Fst and f3 statistics with
# respect to the amount of genetic drift in both lineages
Ne_grid <- c(100, seq(from = 1000, to = 10000, by = 1000))
f3_vs_fst <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, simulate_split, tsplit = 3000)

# and visualization of the f3-vs-Fst comparison
ggplot(f3_vs_fst, aes(Ne, value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45)) +

title: Between-population statistics
text:
Exercise: “Admixture” \(f_3\)
Now let’s explore the application of the \(f_3\) statistic in its other common use, which is an admixture test. To do this, you will need to expand our baseline population model a little bit.
In our model, we still keep the population outgroup, but the X and Y population now merge at a time tmix to form a population mix. Note that due to the way in which slendr currently implements population merges, you will first need to program the split of mix from X at time tmix - 1, followed at time tmix (i.e., immediately in the following generation) by admixture from U at some defined proportion proportion. To approximate the idea of a population merge as closely as possible within the constraints of the slendr interface, program this admixture event so that it ends after a single generation (i.e., it should end at time tmix + 1).

library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)   # manipulating tabular data
library(ggplot2) # data visualization
library(purrr)   # convenient looping functions


tmix <- 2000
prop <- 0.1
Ne <- 5000

outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 5000, time = 10000)
x <- population("x", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
y <- population("y", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
mix <- population("mix", N = Ne, time = tmix + 1, parent = x)

gf <- gene_flow(from = y, to = mix, start = tmix, end = tmix - 1, proportion = prop)

model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, x, y, mix), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

plot_model(model, order = c("outgroup", "x", "mix", "y"), proportions = TRUE)









Exercise
Before we start digging into the limitations of the \(f_3\) statistic as a metric for admixture detection, let’s first create a self-contained function which generalizes our baseline model across three main parameters of interest: the admixture time tmix, the admixture proportion prop, and the effective population size of the admixed population Ne:

compute_admix_f3 <- function(tmix, prop, Ne) {
  outgroup <- population("outgroup", N = 5000, time = 10000)
  x <- population("x", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
  y <- population("y", N = 5000, time = 5000, parent = outgroup)
  mix <- population("mix", N = Ne, time = tmix + 1, parent = x)

  gf <- gene_flow(from = y, to = mix, start = tmix, end = tmix - 1, proportion = prop)
  
  model <- compile_model(list(outgroup, x, y, mix), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(x, 5), list(y, 5), list(mix, 25))

  ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 25e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>% ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  ts_f3(ts, A = samples["mix"], B = samples["x"], C = samples["y"]) %>% mutate(tmix = tmix, prop = prop, Ne = Ne)
}


compute_admix_f3(tmix = 2000, prop = 0.2, Ne = 10000)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  A     B     C              f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     0.000000752  2000   0.2 10000



compute_admix_f3(tmix = 1000, prop = 0.2, Ne = 10000)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  A     B     C              f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     -0.00000658  1000   0.2 10000



compute_admix_f3(tmix = 1, prop = 0.2, Ne = 10000)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  A     B     C             f3  tmix  prop    Ne
  <chr> <chr> <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 mix   x     y     -0.0000109     1   0.2 10000



f3_tmix1 <- map_dfr(seq(1, 1500, by = 100), compute_admix_f3, prop = 0.2, Ne = 5000)


ggplot(f3_tmix1, aes(tmix, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1500))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









From the trend presented by the trajectory of expected \(f_3\) values as a function of the admixture time, we can see that the statistic appears to loose power to detect admixture around 1000 generations “before present” (BP).
Under which conditions would the \(f_3\) statistic gain more power?


Exercise
Fix the tadmix parameter to 1000 generations B.P. (a value at which our previous simulation suggests \(f_3\) starts losing statistical power) and Ne at 5000, and then evaluate a range of admixture proportions prop between 0% and 50% gene flow. Does \(f_3\) pick up the admixture signal for any of these admixture proportions? What does it mean for the ability of \(f_3\) to detect gene flow in our models in general?

f3_prop <- map_dfr(seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.025), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, Ne = 5000)


ggplot(f3_prop, aes(prop, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Exercise
Similarly to how you investigated the detection power of \(f_3\) as a function of admixture proportion for a given value of tmix = 1000 in the previous exercise, repeat this analysis, but now changing the Ne of the mixing population and leaving the prop parameter fixed at prop = 0.2. What do you conclude based on this analysis? Does Ne have an impact on the \(f_3\) admixture detection? If it does, why? (Look at equation XYZ.)

f3_Ne <- map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.2)


ggplot(f3_Ne, aes(Ne, f3)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1000, 20000))

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









In conclusion, we can confirm that the amount of drift (represented by the Ne parameter) really is what determines whether or not can \(f_3\) detect admixture for a given model (represented by a fixed tmix time and prop admixture proportion). In fact, once we reach a certain size of the admixed population, the \(f_3\) value reaches a stable level below zero.


Exercise (extra challenge)

f3_Ne <- bind_rows(
  map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.1),
  map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.2),
  map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.3),
  map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.4),
  map_dfr(seq(1000, 20000, by = 1000), compute_admix_f3, tmix = 1000, prop = 0.5)
)


ggplot(f3_Ne, aes(Ne, f3, color = factor(prop), group = factor(prop))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1000, 20000))

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









By comparing the relative position of these \(f_3\) curves with respect to the baseline null value of zero, we can see that increasing Ne of the admixed population (and, consequently, decreasing the amount of drift in that population post admixture) increases the statistical power of \(f_3\) to detect admixture even as the admixture proportion prop decreases.

    samples <- ts_names(ts2, split = TRUE)
    
    bind_rows(
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["San"],    X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Mbuti"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Yoruba"], X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Dinka"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"])
    )
  }
) %>% mutate(direction = "MH -> Nea")


result <- rbind(result1, result2)


ggplot(result, aes(W, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ direction)

title: \(f_4\) test of gene flow
section: Exercise 6: Detecting Neanderthal admixture in Europeans
text:
Exercise 6: Detecting Neanderthal admixture in Europeans
Let’s now pretend its about 2008, we sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and we are working on a project that will change human evolution research forever. We also have the genomes of a couple of people from Africa and Europe, which we want to use to answer the most burning question of all evolutionary anthropology: “Do some people living today carry Neanderthal ancestry?”
Perhaps you’ve heard earlier about an \(f_4\) statistic (or its equivalent, the \(D\) statistic) which can be used as a test of “treeness”. As a recap, for some “quartet” of individuals or population samples (whose names can be giving as characters such as “EUR_1” to the ts_f4() function, as you can see in the help page of ?ts_f4), they can be used as a hypothesis test of whether the history of those samples is compatible with there not having been an introgression.
Compute the \(f_4\) test of Neanderthal introgression in EUR individuals using the slendr function ts_f4() (make sure to set mode = "branch" argument to minimize stochastic noise).


Note: By default, each slendr / tskit statistic function operates on mutations, and this will switch them to use branch length (as you might know, \(f\)-statistics are mathematically defined using branch lengths in trees and mode = "branch" does exactly that).
Hint: If you haven’t learned this earlier, to solve this exercise, you want to compute and compare the values of these two statistics:

\(f_4\)(<some African>, <another African>; <Neanderthal>, <Chimp>)
\(f_4\)(<some African>, <a test European>; <Neanderthal>, <Chimp>),

here <individual> can be the name of any individual recorded in your tree sequence, such as names you saw as name column in the table returned by ts_recorded(ts) (i.e. "NEA_1" could be used as a “representative” <Neanderthal> in those equations, similarly for "CHIMP_1" as the fourth sample in the \(f_4\) quarted representing the outgroup).

The first \(f_4\) statistic above is not expected to give values “too different” from 0 (even in case of Neanderthal introgression into Europeans) because we don’t expect two African individuals to differ “significantly” in terms of how much alleles they share with a Neanderthal (because their ancestors never met Neanderthals!). However, the other statistic should be “significantly negative” if there Neanderthal introgression into Europeans happened some time throughout their history.
Is the second of those two statistics “much more negative” than the first, as expected assuming introgression from Neanderthals into Europeans?
Why am I putting “significantly” and “much more negative” in quotes in the previous sentence? What are we missing here for this being a true hypothesis test as you might be accustomed to from computing \(f\)-statistics using a tool such as ADMIXTOOLS? (We hinted at this issue a couple of times earlier.)






NoteClick to see the solution





Compute the difference in the amount of allele sharing between two African individuals and a Neanderthal:

f4_null <- ts_f4(ts, W = "AFR_1", X = "AFR_2", Y = "NEA_1", Z = "CHIMP_1", mode = "branch")
f4_null

Compute the difference in the amount of allele sharing between an African individual vs European individual and a Neanderthal:

f4_alt <- ts_f4(ts, W = "AFR_1", X = "EUR_1", Y = "NEA_1", Z = "CHIMP_1", mode = "branch")
f4_alt

We can see that the second test resulted in an f4 value about ~20 times more negative than the first test, indicating that a European in our test carries “significantly more” Neanderthal alleles compared to the baseline expectation of no introgression established by the comparison to an African …

abs(f4_alt$f4 / f4_null$f4)

… although this is not a real test of significance because we have no Z-score or standard error which would give us something like a p-value for the hypothesis test, this evaluation of statistical expectations and trends using simulations is extremely useful in research, because it allows us to test our ideas on ground-truth models. With empirical data, we rarely (if ever) know exactly what happened. With simulations, we always know which process generated the data and how that process could have influenced our statistics of interest.

title: \(f_4\) test of gene flow
section: Exercise 7: Detecting Neanderthal admixture in Europeans v2.0
text:
Exercise 7: Detecting Neanderthal admixture in Europeans v2.0
The fact that we don’t get something equivalent to a p-value in these kinds of simulations is generally not a problem, because we’re often interested in establishing a trend of a statistic under various conditions, and understand under which conditions and in which way its expected value behaves in a certain way. If statistical noise is a problem, we work around this by computing a statistic on multiple simulation replicates or even increasing the sample sizes.


Note: To see this in practice, you can check out a paper in which I used this approach quite successfully on a related problem.
On top of that, p-value of something like an \(f\)-statistic (whether it’s significantly different from zero) is also strongly affected by quality of the data, sequencing errors, coverage, etc. (which can certainly be examined using simulations!). However, these are aspects of modeling which are quite orthogonal to the problem of investigating the expectations and trends of statistics given some underlying evolutionary model, which is what we’re after in these exercises.
That said, even in perfect simulated data, what exactly does “significantly different from zero compared to some baseline expectation” mean can be blurred by noise with simple single-individual comparisons that we did above. Let’s increase the sample size a bit to see if a statistical pattern expected in \(f_4\) statistic from our Neanderthal introgression model becomes more apparent.
Compute the first \(f_4\) statistic (the baseline expectation between a pair of Africans) and the second \(f_4\) statistic (comparing an African and a European), but this time on all recorded Africans and all recorded Europeans, respectively. Plot the distributions of those two sets of statistics. This should remove most of the evolutionary stochastic noise and make a statistical trend stand out much more clearly.
Hint: Whenever you need to compute something for many things in sequence, looping is very useful. One way to do compute, say, an \(f_4\) statistic over many individuals is by using this kind of pattern using R’s looping function lapply():

# Loop over vector of individual names (variable x) and apply a given ts_f4()
# expression on each individual (note the ts_f4(..., X = x, ...) in the code)
X <- c("ind_1", "ind_2", ...)

list_f4 <- lapply(
  X,
  function(x) ts_f4(ts, W = "AFR_1", X = x, Y = "NEA_1", Z = "CHIMP_1", mode = "branch")
)

# The above gives us a list of data frames, so we need to bind them all into a
# single table for easier interpretation and visualization
df_f4 <- do.call(rbind, list_f4)







NoteClick to see the solution





This gives us list of vectors of the names of all individuals in each population…

sample_sets <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
# ... which we can then access like this
sample_sets$AFR # all Africans
sample_sets$EUR # all Europeans

Let’s compute the \(f_4\) statistic for all Africans…

f4_afr_list <- lapply(
  sample_sets$AFR,
  function(x) ts_f4(ts, W = "AFR_1", X = x, Y = "NEA_1", Z = "CHIMP_1", mode = "branch")
)
# ... and Europeans
f4_eur_list <- lapply(
  sample_sets$EUR,
  function(x) ts_f4(ts, W = "AFR_1", X = x, Y = "NEA_1", Z = "CHIMP_1", mode = "branch")
)

Bind each list of data frames into a single data frame:

f4_afr <- do.call(rbind, f4_afr_list)
f4_eur <- do.call(rbind, f4_eur_list)

# add population columns to each of the two results for easier plotting
f4_afr$pop <- "AFR"
f4_eur$pop <- "EUR"

# bind both tables together
f4_results <- rbind(f4_afr, f4_eur)

Now we can visualize the results:

f4_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(pop, f4, color = pop)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  ggtitle("f4(AFR, EUR; NEA, CHIMP)") +
  theme_bw()

We can see that the \(f_4\) statistic test of Neanderthal introgression in Europeans indeed does give a much more negative distribution of values compared to the baseline expectation which compares two Africans to each other.
This is why simulations are so powerful — we establish models which generate data under known population history, and then we can investigate what would be the values of our statistics of interest under those models (and perhaps guess which models are then closest to the hidden truth behind our empirical data).

title: \(f_4\) test of gene flow
section: Exercise: Trajectory of Neanderthal ancestry in Europe over time
text:
Exercise: Trajectory of Neanderthal ancestry in Europe over time
There used to be a lot of controversy about the question of whether or not did Neanderthal ancestry proportion in Europeans decline or not over the past 40 thousand years (see Figure 1 in this paper and Figure 2 in this paper).
Your simulated tree sequence contains a time-series of European individuals over time. Use the slendr function ts_f4ratio() to compute (and then plot, if you’re familiar with data visualization in R) the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry in Europe over time, commonly designated alpha in the literature. Use \(f_4\)-ratio statistic of the following form:

ts_f4ratio(ts, X = <vector individual names>, A = "NEA_1", B = "NEA_2", C = "AFR_1", O = "CHIMP_1")

If a Neanderthal introgression happened at 3% tens of thousands of years ago, what would you expect the proportion to be in the present day? Lower? About the same?






NoteClick to see the solution






# Extract table with names and times of sampled Europeans (ancient and present day)
eur_inds <- ts_recorded(ts) %>% filter(pop == "EUR")
eur_inds

# Compute f4-ration statistic (this will take ~30s) -- note that we can provide
# a vector of names for the X sample set to the `ts_f4ratio()` function
nea_ancestry <- ts_f4ratio(ts, X = eur_inds$name, A = "NEA_1", B = "NEA_2", C = "AFR_1", O = "CHIMP_1")

# Add the age of each sample to the table of proportions
nea_ancestry$time <- eur_inds$time
nea_ancestry

nea_ancestry %>%
  ggplot(aes(time, alpha)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linetype = 2, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  xlim(40000, 0) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "time [years ago]", y = "Neanderthal ancestry proportion") +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Neanderthal ancestry proportion in Europeans over time")

# For good measure, let's test the significance of the decline using a linear model
summary(lm(alpha ~ time, data = nea_ancestry))

In conclusion, assuming neutral drift, we don’t expect the Neanderthal trajectory to change, even after tens of thousands of years.

title: \(f_4\) test of gene flow
section: Exercise: How many unique f4 quartets are there?
text:
Exercise: How many unique f4 quartets are there?
If you’ve learned about \(f\)-statistics before, you’ve probably seen various symmetries in \(f_4\) (but also other \(f\)-statistics) depending on the arrangement of the “quartet”. As a trivial example, an \(f_3(A; B, C)\) and \(f_3(A; C, B)\) will give you exactly the same value, and the same thing applies even to more complex \(f\)-statistics like \(f_4\).
Use simulations to compute how many unique \(f_4\) values involving a single quartet are there.
Hint: Draw some trees to figure out why could that be true. Also, when computing ts_f4(), set mode = "branch" to avoid the effect of statistical noise due to mutations.






NoteClick to see the solution






# # install a combinatorics R package
# install.packages("combinat")

library(combinat)

# These are the four samples we can create quartet combinations from:
quartet <- c("AFR_1", "EUR_1", "NEA_1", "CHIMP_1")

# This is how we can generate all permutations:
quartets <- permn(quartet)
quartets

# How many permutations there are in total?
#   4! = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24
factorial(4)

# We should therefore have 24 different quartet combinations of samples
length(quartets)

# Loop across all quartets, computing the corresponding f4 statistic (we want
# to do this using branch lengths, not mutations, as the mutation-based computation
# would involve statistical noise)
all_f4s <- lapply(quartets, function(q) ts_f4(ts, q[1], q[2], q[3], q[4], mode = "branch"))

# Bind the list of f4 results into a single data frame and inspect the results
all_f4s <- bind_rows(all_f4s) %>% arrange(abs(f4))
print(all_f4s, n = Inf)

# Narrow down the results to only unique f4 values
distinct(all_f4s, f4, .keep_all = TRUE)
distinct(all_f4s, abs(f4), .keep_all = TRUE)
